Name: David Tussey
Question: When a fighter jet had a listed max range ceiling, what does that actually mean when the plane or pilot is near that max or possibly over it? Just not recommended or?
Answer: I flew the A-7E for much of my Navy career. The published Service Ceiling in 42,000 feet. Later in my career I did a lot of Post Maintenance Check Flights (PMCF) to verify the aircraft was operating properly following major maintenance, e.g. engine change, major structural inspection, etc. On those PMCFs I used to take the aircraft as high as possible. I was darn lucky if I could reach 42,000 feet. The engine just runs out of thrust at that altitude. There’s simply not enough air. You could indeed fly at 42,000 feet, and maybe you could actually climb a few hundred feet higher if you were lightly loaded. But for all practical reasons, that’s as high as you can go. (Note: I do realize that many of today’s aircraft have much higher (50K+) service ceilings, especially some of the latest bizjets.) Nothing dramatic happens at 42,000 feet. No changes to the airplane’s handling…the engine just runs out of thrust. Control responsiveness diminishes for the same reason. But it’s perfectly flyable. Recommended or not? Not really recommended. Not really necessary. It’s challenging to control the aircraft at that altitude; it just gets “squirrely”. About the only reason to go that high that I can think of is to clear a thunderstorm, but honestly…it’s easier to just steer around it. There’s no tactical reason I know of to get as “high as you can go”. And for the airplane I flew, it just wasn’t very useful. Nothing you can do at 42,000 feet that you can’t do at 41,000 or 40,000 feet…or even in the high 30’s. BTW, when you are flying cross country in the US, if you’re flying up in the high 30k’s, you’re pretty much alone. Not much traffic up there. Great visibility though. ;-)

Question: What if individuals, recently retired F-16 pilots, volunteered their services in Ukraine to expedite F-16 deployment? Or create an expeditionary unit of former and current F-16 pilots from countries that are un-aligned with Russia?
Answer: Well that would certainly expedite the introduction of the F-16, as well as improve the overall effectiveness of their employment. However, as Peter Webb points out in his answer, such a move would likely be viewed by Russia as NATO intervention into the war. And that could have major consequences for escalation and retaliation. That, in a nutshell, is the challenge with this conflict. NATO and other allied forces could likely easily overwhelm the Russian forces in Ukraine with a full deployment of NATO forces. However, Russia is an unstable country with unstable leadership and and arsenal of tactical and strategic nuclear weapons. Thus the problem with nukes — do they deter war or make it more likely. And no one on either side wants to find out. If Russia were being routed on the eastern battlefields of Ukraine, what might they do? Would they break out and use their tactical nuclear weapons? Would they strike at European cities? Would China and North Korea intervene? Difficult to know, and dangerous to proceed without knowing.

Question: Will soaring hours help me get a pilot spot in the military, or do I need a PPL?
Answer: Neither will help you get a pilot spot. Military pilots are officers first, and pilots later. First you have to complete an officer commissioning program and earn a college degree. Three paths: ROTC, Service Academy, or Officer Candidate School. Then you have to graduate high enough in your class to earn selection for flight school. Then, of course, you have to complete flight school. There is zero guarantee that when you enter an officer commissioning program that you will get flight school. I wrote a previous answer that’s related to this question. Bottom line - previous flying time has near-zero impact on completing military flight school. Helpful for sure, but does not make even a minor difference, and in some cases it hurts by learning bad habits. Check it out. Want to be military pilot, complete college with the best grades possible, complete a commissioning program with the best scores possible…then you improve your chances greatly of getting selected for flight school.

Question: What is the purpose of having both a popular vote and an Electoral College? Could one system be used instead of both?
Answer: Originally the idea was that the Electoral College would literally “pick” the President. The states would vote for their Electors, and all the Electors would gather in Washington D.C. and decide who they wanted as President. Think of it as the Shareholders of a Corporation voting to select the next CEO. That was the idea. It was kind of a compromise from the English system of Parliament + Monarch. Today, that idea is wholly outmoded, and we should just go to a straight national popular vote. But unfortunately, it will take the GOP loosing the EC while winning the popular vote before they admit it’s a flawed system. That almost happened with Kerry v. Bush, but alas Ohio went for Bush…barely. Had that been otherwise, Kerry would have won the EC but lost the popular vote to Bush. God I wish that had happened.

Question: Can I join the military and be a fighter pilot with an atrial septal defect (ASD) surgery? (If you ask how long ago it was 3-4 years ago)?
Answer: While I can’t say for sure, and it varies from country to country, I’d have to say that it is highly unlikely. Heart health is paramount for any pilot regardless of aircraft type. High altitude flying, high G maneuvering, vertigo, and high stress levels make significant demands on the cardiovascular system, not to mention situations such as an ejection, survival at sea, being a POW…and aging. The US military takes a very hard look at the health of flight school candidates. Their approach deems that you have to be in damn near perfect health, at least at the start. Because by the time you’re 40 yrs old, there’s no doubt that you will be less than perfect. So the policy is be especially tough on medical requirements for admission. I would say it is highly unlikely that given you have had ASD surgery that you would be approved for military flight school. Having said that, I would not overlook some other amazing career opportunities with the military, including many that are even aviation related, such as aircraft maintenance, intelligence, and cyber.

Question: Can French fighter jets do midair refueling from American tanker aircraft, and vice versa?
Answer: Yes they can. Most USAF tanker aircraft have the capability to provide refueling either via the probe-drogue method, or via the boom method. All USAF aircraft, including fighter jets, use the boom method. It provides a higher flow rate for refueling. However, aircraft in the USN, USMC, and may allied nations use the probe-drogue method. So USAF tanker aircraft also provide that method of refueling, often via a refueling store on the outer wing station, such that they can maintain both the probe-drogue and boom methods. On dedicated tanker missions for the USN, USMC, or other allied nations, a USAF tanker will configure a “drogue” onto the base of the boom, and provide refueling that way. Since Desert Storm in the late 90s, the emphasis on joint warfare planning and operations has increased enormously. (A hard lesson learned from Desert Storm). So today, the alternate refueling methods are much more widely available than in the past. As we used to say when I flew the A-7E for the US Navy. All you had to do to convert to the USAF A-7D was change the sex. ;-)

Question: Is it true that even though Lockheed Martin designed the F-35, the US government has some sort of ownership over the F-35 program?
Answer: Yes. Of course. Full ownership. Lockheed Martin developed the F-35 for the US Government’s Department of Defense under contract. That contract specifies that the US government owns what LM developed as well as the intellectual property. There are sometimes where there is a cooperative agreement between the manufacturer and the US Government where an item is purchased, but the manufacturer owns the patent or intellectual property. Drug development is one such area. This approach can be used to reduce the cost of the initial purchase (as the IP is quite valuable), but does not give the Government full control over the production and sale of the product. For items relating to national defense, that’s typically not acceptable.
